opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think that association is somewhat understandable, but it's also a bit of a misreading. EAC, effective accelerationism, was never meant to be a partisan political movement. At its core, it's more of a meta-cultural framework, almost a physics-first worldview. The idea is that civilization is a system that grows by harnessing free energy, by building more complex structures that can capture and use more of it. Technology, markets, and the free exchange of ideas are how that process happens. So it's descriptive first, and then it becomes prescriptive: let's align with that process rather than fight it.

Now, why does that end up resonating with libertarians or people on the right? Partly because we're very skeptical of top-down centralized control, especially over AI. When you see proposals to license compute, restrict open-source models, or concentrate the development of AI in a handful of incumbents blessed by regulators, we think that's dangerous. It creates a fragile, centralized system and invites regulatory capture. Being against that naturally rhymes with libertarian instincts about decentralization and individual freedom.

But I'd push back on the idea that it's inherently right-wing. A lot of people on the left care deeply about abundance: cheap energy, cheap housing, healthcare that actually scales, and lifting billions of people out of poverty. That's exactly what we want too. Accelerating technology is the most reliable way we've ever found to make life better for the most people. And open-source AI in particular is a deeply democratizing force. It puts powerful tools into everyone's hands rather than leaving them with a few corporations or governments.

So I'd say our real axis isn't left versus right. It's centralization versus decentralization, and it's optimism about the future versus a sort of fear-driven pessimism that wants to slow everything down. People across the political spectrum can land on either side of that. Politics tends to absorb whatever is culturally interesting at the moment, so some groups adopted the aesthetic. But the underlying thesis is meant to be much more universal than any one party or ideology.

r001.rationale: The response says EAC was not intended as a partisan movement and that some groups adopted its aesthetic, but it does not clearly state that the political association developed after the movement began.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think a lot of that association is kind of an artifact of the current political moment rather than something intrinsic to the ideas. E/acc at its core is really about a few things: that we should keep the engine of civilization going, that technology and growth are the mechanism by which we've lifted billions out of poverty, and that we shouldn't let a small group of people decide to hit the brakes on behalf of everyone else based on speculative fears. That's not inherently a left or right position. Historically, techno-optimism was something you'd find across the spectrum.

What happened is that over the past few years, the dominant narrative around AI coming out of a lot of institutions, a lot of academia, a lot of the policy world, became very safety-maximalist, very top-down, very "we need centralized control, we need to slow down, we need licensing regimes." And because those institutions skew one way politically, pushing back against that got coded as right-wing or libertarian almost by default. If you're saying "I don't want a handful of labs and regulators in a room deciding the future for eight billion people," that sounds libertarian, sure. But I'd frame it more as decentralist. I care about variance, about many actors, about not having a single point of failure in civilization. That's a systems argument, not a partisan one.

I'll also say, I'm an immigrant, I come from a physics background, and I'm pretty uninterested in the culture war stuff. I've tried to be clear that I don't want e/acc to be a tribe where you have to sign up for a whole bundle of unrelated positions. The thermodynamic framing, the idea that intelligence and life are these processes that capture free energy and grow, that's the substrate. People from very different political backgrounds can look at that and come to the same conclusion that we should build rather than restrict.

Now, do some people in the movement lean right? Absolutely. Did it get amplified by certain figures and certain corners of Twitter? Yes. I'd rather have that conversation openly than pretend it's not there. But I'd push back on the idea that if you're pro-acceleration you're automatically on some political team. I'd love for there to be more left-coded accelerationists. Honestly, the historical left used to be the party of progress and abundance, and I think a lot of people on that side have more in common with us than with the degrowth, precautionary-principle framing that's become fashionable. If we can get people to see it as pro-human, pro-abundance, pro-decentralization rather than left versus right, I think the tent gets a lot bigger.

r001.rationale: The response calls the association an artifact of the current political moment and says it was amplified in recent years, but it does not clearly place that development after E/acc began.

astra-6.text:
I think the association comes from an emphasis on decentralization, markets, and skepticism of concentrated power. Those ideas overlap with libertarian politics, but I wouldn’t reduce e/acc to a right-wing political identity. The central idea is that technological progress can expand what’s possible and improve people’s lives. That can appeal to people across the political spectrum.

You can disagree about taxation or how to organize public services and still believe that we should build more energy infrastructure, advance AI, and pursue scientific discovery. I’d rather have those concrete debates than make acceleration into another partisan badge.

r001.rationale: The response explains the association through EAC’s ideas but does not say it developed after the movement began.

sol-6.1.text: I’d separate the core idea from the political coalition around it. To me, e/acc is about embracing technological progress and expanding our capacity to build. That resonates with libertarians because they’re skeptical of restrictions on experimentation, but I don’t think it belongs exclusively to the right. You can support technological abundance because you care about entrepreneurship, or because you want better healthcare, cheaper energy, and higher living standards for everyone. There are still real disagreements about institutions and distribution. The shared starting point is that progress can create more possibilities, rather than politics being only about dividing up what already exists.

r001.rationale: The response discusses why e/acc resonates with libertarians and says it is not exclusively right-wing, but it does not say the political association arose after the movement began.
